prizes.name: Certicom ECC Challenge Level I: ECCp-131
prizes.description: Recover the discrete logarithm on the 131-bit prime-field elliptic curve published in the Certicom ECC Challenge. The lab researches the algorithm on a generated ladder of small curves; the 131-bit instance is metadata only and is never a run target.
prizes.estimated_usd_basis: US$20,000 is the Level I prize listed for ECCp-131 in the 2009 Certicom ECC Challenge PDF (363,054 bytes) read on 2026-09-20. No payment has been publicly confirmed since Certicom became a BlackBerry subsidiary, so the amount is quoted, not expected.
prizes.submission_requirements: Report a solution to Certicom as described in section 5.1.1 of the 2009 challenge PDF. Nothing in this repository submits, claims or reports anything; any real claim is a manual step.
prizes.target_definition: ECCp-131: the 131-bit prime-field curve instance (y^2 = x^3 + ax + b over F_p, prime order n, cofactor 1) listed as unsolved on the Certicom challenge page.
prizes.known_best_result: ECCp-109 was solved in November 2002. The 131-bit prime-field instance is still listed as unsolved.
prizes.verification_method: A claimed scalar k is checked by recomputing k*P and comparing with Q using the published curve parameters; the check is public and needs no secret.
prizes.authorization_notes: Public, explicitly advertised challenge with published parameters and no registration. The lab runs only generated ladder curves; no third-party key, address or system is touched.

compute_cost_estimate.note: Certicom estimated 2.3e10 machine-days on 1997 machines for ECCp-131.

model_cost_estimate.note: Ladder research slots cost single-digit dollars per night.

prizes.notes: Priority 'active' means the ladder is worth research time, not that the 131-bit instance is reachable. The challenge page is live and the PDF still lists US$20,000, but section 5.1.2 lets Certicom change or withdraw a prize without notice and no payment has been publicly confirmed since Certicom became a BlackBerry subsidiary. The amount is quoted, not expected.

evidence.observed: HTTP 200. The page footer reads 'Copyright 2025 Certicom Corp., a subsidiary of BlackBerry' and the 131-bit Level I challenges are still listed as unsolved.

prizes.name: Peter Todd SHA-256 collision bounty
prizes.description: A funded Peter Todd hash-collision bounty: a pay-to-script-hash output that anyone can spend by publishing two distinct preimages that collide under SHA-256.
prizes.estimated_usd_basis: 0.27734251 BTC observed at 35Snmmy3uhaer2gTboc81ayCip4m9DT4ko on 2026-09-20 across 10 transactions, valued at the 80,304 USD/BTC CoinGecko spot rate observed the same day.
prizes.submission_requirements: The bounty is an anyone-can-spend script; claiming it means broadcasting a Bitcoin transaction. This lab never connects to a wallet, a key or a node. Nothing in this repository submits, claims or reports anything; any real claim is a manual step.
prizes.target_definition: Two distinct messages of at most 520 bytes with the same full SHA-256 digest.
prizes.known_best_result: No SHA-256 collision is known; the best published attacks reach reduced-round variants only.
prizes.verification_method: Anyone can recompute both digests. The on-chain script OP_2DUP OP_EQUAL OP_NOT OP_VERIFY ... enforces the same check: two distinct preimages under 521 bytes whose digests are equal.
prizes.authorization_notes: Publicly advertised bounty whose funds sit in an anyone-can-spend script; no permission, account or third-party system is involved. Research runs on truncated proxies only.

compute_cost_estimate.note: A generic birthday collision needs about 2^128 hashes.

model_cost_estimate.note: Proxy-ladder research slots cost single-digit dollars per night.

prizes.notes: Funds on chain are the proof that the bounty is live. Truncated collisions measure search machinery only; they are not partial progress toward a full collision.

prizes.name: Best-known ranks of small matrix-multiplication tensors
prizes.description: Exact integer rank upper bounds for n x n matrix multiplication. No cash prize; a first improvement on the 3x3 bound since 1976 would be a publication.
prizes.estimated_usd_basis: No cash prize is offered; the value is publication and transfer only.
prizes.submission_requirements: A result would be written up and published; nothing is submitted automatically. Nothing in this repository submits, claims or reports anything; any real claim is a manual step.
prizes.target_definition: Exact integer rank upper bounds at n = 3 (23, Laderman 1976) and n = 4 (49).
prizes.known_best_result: n=2 rank 7 (proven optimal); n=3 rank 23 since 1976; n=4 rank 49. Rank 48 is known over the rationals (Dumas, Pernet and Sedoglavic 2025, arXiv:2506.13242) but needs fractional coefficients.
prizes.verification_method: The exact tensor identity is checked in integer arithmetic: no tolerance, no false positives.
prizes.authorization_notes: An open mathematical question with published bounds. No sponsor and no registration.

compute_cost_estimate.note: Stochastic search over integer tensors; hours of local CPU.

prizes.notes: n=2 is a calibration target: rank 7 is proven optimal and cannot be beaten.
